title: State Schools: GCSE and A-level Arts Subjects

contributions.text: To ask His Majesty’s Government what steps they are taking to increase entries for arts subjects at GCSE and A Level in state schools.
contributions.name: Baroness Keeley

contributions.text: My Lords, since the first Labour Arts Minister, Jennie Lee, through to our current Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy, there has been a driving passion that all our children should be given the kind of education that used to be the monopoly of the privileged few. That principle remains as important today as it was in 1965. However, due to the education policies of the Conservative-led Government since 2010, for too many young people in state schools, an arts-rich education exists only for those whose parents can pay for extracurricular tuition. Arts education is not just about preparing future artists; it helps young people to develop creativity, confidence, communication skills and critical thinking, whatever careers they eventually pursue. It is vital to the economic success of our country. The creative industries are one of the UK’s great success stories. They contribute almost £146 billion to our economy and employ 2.4 million people. They are globally competitive and increasingly important to the UK’s future prosperity. They also depend on a highly skilled workforce. Around two-thirds of creative workers hold degree-level qualifications, and Skills England predicts that most future
contributions.name: Baroness Keeley

contributions.text: I congratulate the noble Baroness on her well-prepared and interesting opening speech, and I certainly look forward to the answers from the Minister. I also just needed to say how much I regret that the Chair is sitting as Chair of this Committee and not making a major contribution to the debate—I wonder whether we could prevail on her to do so later. There is a familiar saying attributed to William Butler Yeats: “Education is not the filling of a pail but the lighting of a fire”, and few things ignite that fire quite like music, drama, dance or art. I had the privilege to be Secretary of State for National Heritage when John Major’s National Lottery began to transform investment in Britain’s cultural institutions. Sir Ernest Hall, a great man, famously compared its contribution to that of the Medici family in Florence, burnishing our great national treasure houses. Yet we probably paid insufficient attention to nurturing the next generation of talent. The British Academy should be commended for its important work championing arts education. The research paints a troubling picture, with the proportion of GCSE entries in arts subjects falling from 7% in 2010 to just 5% in 2026. The
contributions.name: Baroness Bottomley of Nettlestone

contributions.text: I congratulate the noble Baroness on obtaining this debate. The decline in the number of young people taking arts subjects at GCSE and A-level is deeply concerning not just for the arts but for the future of our economy and the opportunities available to young people. We have seen a substantial fall in entries for subjects such as music, drama, and design and technology over the past decade, which is not surprising given the scant regard paid by Governments to our fantastically talented population. While there are a number of reasons for this, the impact of decisions made within schools about which subjects to offer, how they are funded and how they are valued has taken its toll. We need to distinguish between a lack of demand among pupils and a lack of opportunity because, if a school no longer offers music GCSE or cannot afford a specialist teacher, entries will inevitably fall, but that tells us very little about whether young people actually want to study the subject. As has been said, this matters particularly in state schools, because families who can afford private lessons, specialist tuition and extracurricular activities compensate for what is missing from the curriculum,
contributions.name: Baroness Featherstone

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the noble Baroness, Lady Keeley, for this debate, and look forward to us meeting again next week at the debate of the noble Baroness, Lady Caine of Kentish Town, on the creative industries. As ever, I declare my interest, in that I am a teacher of GCSE and A-level DT at a state school. I am also teaching food at the moment, much to the amusement of my wife. My son did art through to foundation level and my daughter is doing GCSE at the moment, so I have several dogs in this fight. The need for teaching outstanding art in state schools is easy. We need, as everyone has said, a teacher who is an expert in their subject and who loves it. We need space to work but also space to exhibit, and to inspire the next cohort. We need materials and a Department for Education that thinks that this is important. If we want teachers who know and love the subject, the best place to get them is the workplace. I got into teaching in my 50s via Schools Direct, which was the government scheme whereby the school employed you, the Government paid you and you got your university fees paid. Unfortunately, nowadays, that is open only to people who are already in schools to upskill them so
contributions.name: Lord Hampton

contributions.text: My Lords, I, too, thank the noble Baroness, Lady Keeley, for introducing this debate and giving us an opportunity to discuss this. There is a strange contradiction at the centre of any debate about young people and the creative arts. Outside schools, we have a vibrant, excellent, growing and glowing group of young people with immense talent who are practising arts wherever they are. Inside school, there is a decline in the number of hours that it is taught and the number of people taking exams. I cannot think of any other subject for which that is the case. If they do not teach physics in school, they are not going around doing physics outside of school—and the same can be true for any other subject. You might argue, “If they are doing it without school, what is the problem? We are world-leading in the creative industries. It is not as though what does not happen in school feeds to a paucity of expertise outside school”. But exams matter in the mix of things that are part of this debate. They matter, first, because they are a key to some routes to the creative industries that would not be available if you do not have a GCSE or A-level. They are the key to higher education, the cons
contributions.name: Baroness Morris of Yardley

contributions.text: My Lords, I declare an interest as chair of the University of the Arts London. The pipeline into the university through schools is hugely important. I am not alone in suggesting that the decline in arts education in our state schools is deeply concerning. We have heard from my noble friend Lady Keeley about the significant decline in numbers over many years. It is a sad fact that many schools no longer offer GCSEs and A-levels in key creative subjects. Most troublingly, schools in our most deprived areas are the least likely to offer these opportunities. While recruitment to arts teaching has improved recently, as I understand it, too many pupils are still taught by non-specialist teachers. Every child, regardless of background, deserves access to a broad and balanced education in which creativity plays a central role. Creative education should not be an optional extra. I therefore urge the Government, when they publish their revised national curriculum, to take four steps: first, guarantee an entitlement to creative arts education through to at least key stage 3, but ideally to key stage 4, with opportunities to pursue creative subjects throughout a young person’s education; secon
contributions.name: Lord Isaac

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank the noble Baroness, Lady Keeley, for securing this debate. My starting point is that I believe all children and young people will benefit from school time spent on the arts, film, music and drama, regardless of whether they go on to make it one of their exam picks, let alone choose it as a career. Creative subjects should be for all in the same way in which we believe all children benefit from PE without expecting them to go on and do an exam in it. However, this debate is about how we get more young people not just enjoying the benefits of a creative education but selecting it as a GCSE and/or A-level. We have heard many sensible questions raised but I want to look at this from the perspective of the young person themselves. My core argument today is that we cannot expect young people to aspire to careers they have never encountered. When we talk about careers in the arts, inevitably it is the stars people think of first, and it is absolutely right to dream of that BAFTA or BRIT award. But go backstage at the Royal Opera House and you discover an extraordinary industrial operation. Yet, how many young people know these sorts of careers exist? How many teenagers i
contributions.name: Lord Doyle

contributions.text: My Lords, I congratulate my noble friend on securing this debate in the week when we have had two iconic examples of British creative power, with the announcement of the new James Bond and the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. These are two examples of the global power of our creative industries, built on the imagination and, as others have said, resulting in a sector that is worth £146 billion and growing at a fast rate each year. I have never agreed with a utilitarian view of education which is focused purely on what jobs it should lead to, and which has led to a focus for decades purely on STEM subjects. I think we have underfocused on the human need for children to use their imagination and develop their maturity. However, with the advent of AI, it is become absolutely clear that knowing and processing information is no longer sufficient; what is needed is judgment, original thought and the ability to engage with people, and the arts help to foster that, whatever career you choose to take. I was struck by Professor Carl Benedikt Frey of Oxford University saying that highly talented people in the creative industries will be the irreplaceable superstars of the future while those wh
contributions.name: Baroness Bi

contributions.text: My Lords, it is extremely worrying that A-level entries for certain arts subjects between 2022 and 2026 declined so dramatically. However, the problem, and we have heard this elsewhere, begins at an earlier stage. Most children are not going to suddenly switch to music and the arts if they only encounter them as teenagers. I am often asked about the perceived “difficulty” of modern music, and I point out that the answer lies in the exact opposite of the old adage, “familiarity breeds contempt”. Familiarity breeds love across the arts. Exposure to the arts needs to begin at primary school at assembly, where children should experience different music every day, and in communal singing. But here, as with later stages of education, there is an imbalance between the state system and the independent sector, despite the fact that around 93% of children attend state schools. There, they are likely to get a fraction of the music tuition available in the independent sector, so disadvantaged students are 39% less likely to take GCSE music. As both this and the last Government have acknowledged, this situation is partially due to a lack of teachers, so I wonder how the Minister can justify the
contributions.name: Lord Berkeley of Knighton

contributions.text: My Lords, in a world increasingly dominated by the current and future capabilities of artificial intelligence, we are sometimes reminded of its frailties—for example, with last week’s Microsoft outage, which left many of us quite pleased and relieved that we had a few hours where we did not have to constantly refresh our email inboxes. It should also serve as a reminder to us that nothing beats the wonder of actual human creativity, a live performance of a play or music, or seeing art, design or an object that has been created by the human imagination and skill. I strongly believe that the creative and artistic sector will not be a nice add-on for our future economy but will be central to that economy and to the growth of our human community. That is why I am delighted to be a trustee of the Old Vic Theatre, which I declare, and was pleased to attend, along with others, the joyful reception here yesterday organised by the Royal Shakespeare Company, where the Question in this timely debate brought by my noble friend Lady Keeley seemed to have such relevance, and where the brilliant actor Dame Harriet Walter made much the same point about the importance of human interaction. It is ri
contributions.name: Lord John of Southwark

contributions.text: My Lords, I, too, congratulate my noble friend Lady Keeley on securing another debate and her indefatigable leadership in pursuing opportunities to discuss this area. The national curriculum review was tasked with addressing the skills and aptitudes needed for young people’s futures in this fast-paced changing world, one where they consume, produce and watch content on screens constantly. However, the philosophical position informing the review—of evolution, not revolution—was taken literally and only those subject areas already delivered within the curriculum were addressed. Leading institutions wanting to prosecute the case for including film, media and TV studies were advised not to do so, because it would mean that another art subject would have to be taken out. As a result, film, media and TV studies at GCSE and A-level are available but have always stayed outside the curriculum and performance management measures, and remain so, despite being vital for media literacy, creative education and the skills that our future economy needs, not just for the creative industries but right across the economy. There are innumerable creative roles right across different sectors. There was
contributions.name: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town

contributions.text: My Lords, I congratulate the noble Baroness, Lady Keeley, on introducing this debate so well. If everything were rosy in the arts education garden, we would not have had the delivery last week of the open letter by Arts and Minds, which represents so many experts, to the Department for Education, asking for the Government to fulfil their commitment to restore the value of the arts in schools. As I said in the recent debate of the noble Baroness, Lady Featherstone, after years of the arts being diminished in schools, there will inevitably be an institutional bias—which the noble Baroness, Lady Keeley, touched on—alongside the practical obstacles that will take a lot to shift. The Government have a huge role to play in doing so. The recent Teacher Tapp surveys confirm the extent of the challenge. Only 7% of schools expect to increase time spent on creative subjects over the next two years. Meanwhile, 92% say a lack of funding has negatively affected arts provision, including facilities, and 45% of schools in the most deprived areas cannot offer even one art subject at GCSE or BTEC level because of the shortage of teachers. Bursaries for all art subjects need to be reintroduced. The p
contributions.name: The Earl of Clancarty

contributions.text: My Lords, I congratulate my noble friend Lady Keeley on securing such an important debate. Let me add a further statistic to the many remarkable statistics that noble Lords have shared so far: the proportion of students studying AS-levels in all subjects who qualify for free school meals is currently 16%, but for music AS-level it is 3.7%. That is another marked inequality, using the measure of free school meals, which highlights differential access to arts education in different schools in different parts of the country. The challenge is not simply to persuade more students to study arts and music; it is to introduce structural incentives that should encourage schools to prioritise subjects that would be counted within Progress 8, the English baccalaureate and performance measures. Therefore, in the spirit of constructive endeavour, I will suggest a number of effective ideas to improve participation without diluting academic excellence or creating significant additional costs. The Government could consider introducing an arts premium linked to school accountability measures. This would be a measurable creative performance score; schools could get recognition and funding for the pr
contributions.name: Lord Forbes of Newcastle

contributions.text: My Lords, as I listened to this debate, I was astounded by the degree of harmony that had broken out and by the fact that every original point I had has been picked off one by one. I will give just a few thoughts. When I look at GCSEs and A-levels, I am not that bothered by the figures, but I am particularly interested in the skills that come with the person who teaches them. If you are going to encourage people even to do this as a hobby, we need to remember what we have learned from sports—I think the noble Lord, Lord Doyle, mentioned this—which is that anybody who partakes in sports generally has better results in education. The same is true of anything else that gives them that degree of positiveness and that reassurance that opens them up to learning. It is about the fact that you can get somebody in there who knows what they are doing, even if it is only at the introductory level. That first step of any journey and the most difficult part—why not go to another cliché?—which is getting an introduction, means they will be open to taking it further. There are other points. I received the UK Music brief. If we are looking at music, teach people to play guitars first, not violins.
contributions.name: Lord Addington

contributions.text: My Lords, this is a valuable debate but time is brief. Arts and creative subjects are building blocks of individual fulfilment, economic success and civilisation itself, so it is right that in compulsory schooling every child should have a broad and rich curriculum, including in arts and creative subjects. Your Lordships can find me on record on this over many years. I have checked the source data. The good news is that art is in rude health in schools. GCSE entries dipped between 2000 and 2010, but they recovered and in 2026 were as strong as in 2000. I see art rooms everywhere in constant use, and we should celebrate that. Elsewhere, the picture is more mixed—by the way, some of the same trends are also visible in Scotland and Wales. In music and drama, factoring in the shift from GCSEs and A-levels into BTECs and similar programmes, the decline is smaller than many believe but still very real. It is design and technology that has really been hammered. In 2000, around two-thirds of students took it at GCSE; now it is under 15%. Despite what is so often asserted, most of that drop happened before the EBacc measure, not after it. This reflects serious errors made by the Labour Gove
contributions.name: Baroness Spielman

contributions.who: Baroness in Waiting/Government Whip (Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath) (Lab)
contributions.text: My Lords, I seem to have made more notes than what is actually in my speech, so please bear with me and I will do my very best. I am grateful to my noble friend Lady Keeley for securing this debate and to all noble Lords who have contributed. I took a long-standing personal interest in arts education as a Back-Bencher, and I have a daughter who was fortunate enough to go to the BRIT School, mentioned by the noble Baroness, Lady Bottomley. As I have been involved in so many debates, it is a pleasure to see all the noble Lords in the Room, with their particular interests and areas of profound and deep expertise. Every young person, regardless of background, should have the opportunity to study and succeed in creative subjects, including GCSEs and A-levels. The arts enrich lives, develop confidence and communication, and nurture the talent on which our creative industries depend. Those industries contribute approximately £145 billion to the economy and have grown four times faster than the wider economy since 2010. contributions.name: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
